body:
Sahajanand Swami and the Growth of the Tradition

Swaminarayan, also known as Sahajanand Swami (1781–1830), became the central figure of an influential religious movement in Gujarat during the early 19th century.

He was born at Chhapaiya, near Ayodhya, and is traditionally associated with the childhood name Ghanshyam and the ascetic name Nilkanth. After travelling as a renunciant, he became a disciple of Ramanand Swami and later assumed leadership of the religious community associated with him.

Under Sahajanand Swami, the movement expanded especially in Gujarat, including Saurashtra and Kutch. It combined devotion, ethical discipline, religious teaching and the establishment of permanent institutions.

Religious Beliefs and Everyday Conduct

The Swaminarayan tradition emphasised devotion to God together with disciplined personal conduct. Religious life was expected to influence a follower's daily behaviour, not remain confined to prayer or temple attendance.

Its ethical teachings discouraged violence, theft, intoxicants and conduct regarded as harmful to individuals or families. The movement also promoted religious gatherings, congregational singing and adherence to an organised code of conduct.

This organisational character distinguished the Swaminarayan tradition from the individual poetic contributions of saints such as Narsinh Mehta and Akho.

Shikshapatri and Vachanamrut

Two important texts are particularly useful for identifying the teachings of the Swaminarayan tradition.

TextNatureImportant fact
ShikshapatriCode of religious and ethical conductComposed by Sahajanand Swami at Vadtal in 1826; contains 212 Sanskrit verses
VachanamrutCollection of religious discourses and spiritual explanationsRecords teachings delivered during 1819–1829 and compiled by leading disciples

The distinction concerns both authorship and content. The Shikshapatri was composed as a code of conduct by Sahajanand Swami. The Vachanamrut preserves his spoken teachings as recorded and organised by disciples.

Shikshapatri: 1826 and 212 Verses

The Shikshapatri was composed in Sanskrit at Vadtal in 1826 and contains 212 verses. Its subject is the ethical and religious conduct of followers.

Temples and Centres in Gujarat

The tradition established major temples and enduring religious centres. Important examples include:

  • Kalupur, Ahmedabad: An important early Swaminarayan temple established in 1822.
  • Vadtal: An important temple centre established in 1824 and the place where the Shikshapatri was composed in 1826.
  • Bhuj: An important centre of the tradition in Kutch.
  • Gadhada and Junagadh: Important places associated with Swaminarayan religious activity and institutions.

Ahmedabad and Vadtal also became important seats of religious leadership. The existence of temples, teachers, recognised scriptures and organised congregations helped the movement continue beyond the founder's lifetime.

Social and Cultural Influence

In early-19th-century Gujarat, the movement encouraged moral discipline and sought to discourage practices such as female infanticide and sati. Its teachings also emphasised nonviolence and avoidance of harmful habits.

The movement helped create communities organised around shared worship, religious instruction and expectations of conduct. It also encouraged devotional literature and music, including the work of saint-poets associated with the tradition.

These reforms require careful interpretation. Opposition to particular harmful customs did not mean that every restriction based on gender or caste disappeared from the movement or wider society. The historical contribution should be understood through its specific teachings and activities rather than an unlimited claim of social equality.

Prelims focus

  • Sahajanand Swami, known as Swaminarayan, lived from 1781 to 1830.
  • He was associated with Ramanand Swami and the expansion of the movement in Gujarat.
  • The Kalupur temple in Ahmedabad was established in 1822.
  • Vadtal became an important temple centre in 1824.
  • The Shikshapatri was composed at Vadtal in 1826 and contains 212 Sanskrit verses.
  • Trap: The Vachanamrut is a collection of recorded discourses, not another name for the Shikshapatri.

[Sources: University of Oxford, Bodleian Libraries, Shikshapatri Viewing, About the Shikshapatri, and Bodleian Libraries Send Sacred Hindu Text Shikshapatri on UK Tour to Mark Bicentenary, 24 March 2026; BAPS, Vachanamrut, central scriptures section; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Swaminarayan Sampraday and Gujarat: Religion and Culture, section Swaminarayan pilgrimage centres; University of Oxford research on the Swaminarayan tradition and contested reforms; consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: The Swaminarayan Tradition: Religious Organisation and Social Reform

body:
Bhoja Bhagat: A Saint Who Criticised Hypocrisy

Bhoja Bhagat (1785–1850), also known as Bhojo Bhagat, was a Gujarati saint-poet associated with Devki Galol, near Jetpur, and Fatehpur, near Amreli in Saurashtra.

His teachings emphasised devotion, moral conduct and the need to abandon harmful habits. He criticised superstition, religious pretence, pride and practices that prevented people from recognising genuine spiritual values.

Bhoja Bhagat is particularly remembered for his chabkhas. These are forceful, memorable verses that expose faults in human behaviour. Their sharp language is intended to awaken moral understanding rather than merely entertain listeners.

The association between Bhoja Bhagat and chabkhas is comparable to the association between Akho and chhappas, but the two are different literary figures and are identified with different characteristic forms.

Jalaram Bapa: Devotion Expressed Through Feeding Others

Jalaram Bapa (1799–1881) was a prominent saint of Saurashtra associated with Virpur in present-day Rajkot district.

His devotional life centred on Rama, remembrance of God's name and service to people in need. His wife, Virbai, played an important part in this tradition of hospitality and service.

Jalaram is particularly remembered for establishing a sadavrat, a tradition of providing food to visitors, saints, travellers and needy people. This service became the defining feature of the religious centre associated with him at Virpur.

Meaning of Sadavrat

A sadavrat is an ongoing charitable arrangement for providing food. In Jalaram's tradition, feeding others was understood as a practical expression of devotion and compassion.

The Guru-Disciple Relationship

An important connection between the two saints is that Jalaram Bapa was a disciple of Bhoja Bhagat. Bhoja Bhagat's religious centre was associated with Fatehpur near Amreli, while Jalaram's service tradition became associated with Virpur.

Their relationship shows how a shared concern for faith and moral conduct could be expressed in different ways. Bhoja Bhagat became especially known through corrective poetry; Jalaram became especially known through continuing charitable service.

Social Importance of Their Teachings

Bhoja Bhagat's poetry sought to change behaviour by questioning hypocrisy and superstition. Jalaram's sadavrat responded directly to the needs of hungry travellers and other people.

Both illustrate the close relationship between religion and everyday ethical responsibility in Gujarati saint traditions. However, their literary and charitable contributions should be distinguished from the organised religious institutions of the Swaminarayan movement.

Prelims focus

  • Bhoja Bhagat lived from 1785 to 1850.
  • He was associated with Devki Galol and Fatehpur near Amreli.
  • His characteristic literary form was the chabkha.
  • Jalaram Bapa lived from 1799 to 1881 and is associated with Virpur in Rajkot district.
  • Jalaram was a devotee of Rama, a disciple of Bhoja Bhagat and closely associated with the sadavrat tradition.
  • Trap: Bhoja Bhagat is associated particularly with chabkhas; Jalaram Bapa is associated particularly with charitable feeding at Virpur.

[Sources: Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Bhojo Bhagat and Bhakt Jalaram, particularly their accounts of Fatehpur, Virpur, chabkhas and the guru-disciple relationship; consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Bhoja Bhagat was Jalaram Bapa’s guru: Bhoja is remembered for chabkha poetry against hypocrisy, Jalaram for charitable feeding.
pictures.caption: Bhoja Bhagat was Jalaram Bapa's spiritual teacher, but each is remembered for a different contribution.

title: Bhoja Bhagat and Jalaram Bapa: Moral Teaching and Service

body:
A Woman Saint of Saurashtra

Ganga Sati was a Gujarati woman saint-poet associated with the 19th century. She is particularly connected with Samadhiyala in present-day Bhavnagar district.

She belonged to a devotional household in which religious singing, spiritual discipline and the guidance of a teacher were important. Her husband was Kahlasang Bhagat, who is also remembered as a saint.

Ganga Sati's contribution is especially significant because her teachings were preserved in the form of Gujarati bhajans. These songs provided instruction in a language and form that ordinary listeners could understand and remember.

The Relationship Between Ganga Sati and Panbai

Panbai was Ganga Sati's close companion and spiritual disciple. The songs associated with Ganga Sati are remembered as teachings addressed to Panbai.

According to the traditional account, Ganga Sati composed 52 instructional bhajans over 52 days following the death of Kahlasang Bhagat. The number and sequence belong to the established devotional tradition surrounding these songs.

The important distinction is between the roles of the 3 figures:

  • Kahlasang Bhagat: Ganga Sati's husband and a saint associated with the same devotional setting.
  • Ganga Sati: The woman saint-poet whose instructional bhajans became widely known.
  • Panbai: Ganga Sati's disciple and the recipient of her spiritual instruction in the traditional accounts.

Main Teachings in the Bhajans

Ganga Sati's compositions emphasise devotion, spiritual understanding, self-discipline and humility. They also recognise the importance of a genuine spiritual teacher.

Her songs encourage the listener to overcome pride and cultivate steady practice rather than merely display religion outwardly. Their teaching places importance on the condition of the mind and the quality of conduct.

The devotional tradition also emphasises spiritual worth beyond pride in caste or social position. This connects Ganga Sati's work with the wider Bhakti concern for sincere devotion and inner transformation.

Importance in Gujarati Cultural Life

Ganga Sati's bhajans became part of Gujarat's oral devotional heritage. Their continued singing helped preserve religious instruction beyond the original household and its immediate followers.

Her example also shows the important role of women in preserving and transmitting devotional literature. Unlike a temple-based institutional leader, she is primarily remembered through the instruction contained in her songs.

Do Not Confuse the Relationship

Panbai is remembered as Ganga Sati's disciple, not her daughter-in-law. The popular account of 52 bhajans in 52 days is a traditional narrative and should not be presented as a separately verified daily record.

Prelims focus

  • Ganga Sati was a 19th-century Gujarati woman saint-poet.
  • She is associated with Samadhiyala in Bhavnagar district.
  • Her husband was Kahlasang Bhagat.
  • Panbai was her close disciple.
  • The tradition associates Ganga Sati with 52 instructional bhajans composed over 52 days.
  • Trap: Panbai should not be identified as Ganga Sati's daughter-in-law.

[Sources: Gujarati Vishwakosh, entry Bhagat, Kahlasang, sections on Kahlasang Bhagat, Ganga Sati, Panbai and the 52 instructional bhajans; consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Kahlasang Bhagat is Ganga Sati’s husband; Panbai is her disciple, taught through a tradition of 52 instructional bhajans over 52 days.
pictures.caption: The Ganga Sati tradition connects a devotional household with spiritual instruction passed to Panbai.

title: Ganga Sati: Spiritual Instruction Through Gujarati Bhajans

body:
Kabir and the Teaching of the Formless Divine

Kabir was an influential North Indian saint-poet associated broadly with the 15th–16th centuries. His compositions criticised religious hypocrisy, caste pride and excessive dependence on outward rituals.

Kabir taught devotion to a formless Supreme Reality. His verses used religious vocabulary familiar to both Hindus and Muslims, expressing the belief that the Divine could not be restricted to separate community identities.

The Kabir-panth refers to religious traditions that developed around Kabir's teachings. The Bijak is an important collection associated with the Kabir-panth, while verses attributed to Kabir also occur in other compilations, including the Sikh scriptural tradition.

Kabir was not originally a Gujarati saint. His importance to Gujarat includes the influence of his teachings on later local religious and poetic communities.

Ravi-Bhan and the Kabir-Panth Connection

A particularly important Gujarati link is the Ravi-Bhan Sampraday, also called the Ravibhan tradition. It developed within a stream influenced by the Kabir tradition, especially the Ram-Kabiriya branch in Gujarat.

Bhan Saheb (1698–1755) was a major early teacher associated with this Gujarati tradition. His disciple Ravi Saheb (1727–1804) became another prominent saint. The name Ravi-Bhan combines the names of these 2 figures, with the disciple's name appearing first.

The tradition spread through bhajans, spiritual instruction, travelling teachers and religious centres. Its teachings criticised rigid social distinctions and stressed devotion and moral conduct.

Dasi Jivan, also called Dasi Jivan Saheb, was an important later Gujarati saint-poet in the broader Ravi-Bhan spiritual lineage. His devotional poetry expresses both personal love for the Divine and ideas connected with spiritual knowledge.

Although this lineage is connected with Kabir, its later Gujarati poetry includes both Saguna and Nirguna forms of religious expression. Therefore, every poet in the later tradition should not automatically be described as teaching exclusively formless devotion.

The Pranami or Nijanand Tradition

The Pranami Sampraday, also called the Krishna Pranami or Nijanand tradition, has a different historical origin in Gujarat.

Its founding figure was Devchandraji, who established the religious centre known as Navtanpuri Dham, also called Khijada Mandir, at Jamnagar in 1630.

Mahamati Prannath, also known as Prannathji, became an important disciple and major teacher who spread the tradition's ideas. He is particularly associated with its religious literature and the wider propagation of its teachings.

The principal sacred compilation is known as the Tartam Sagar, also called the Kuljam Swarup or Swarup Saheb. It preserves teachings associated with Prannath.

The Pranami tradition is connected with Krishna devotion and teaches spiritual understanding alongside respect for religious truths expressed across different traditions. Its emphasis on broader religious understanding should not be confused with the separate history of Kabir-panth communities.

Founder and Propagator Are Different

Devchandraji is the founding figure of the Nijanand or Krishna Pranami tradition. Prannath was his important disciple and a major propagator. Identifying Prannath as the original founder without qualification confuses their roles.

How the Two Traditions Differ

The Kabir-related Ravi-Bhan tradition developed through a Gujarati saint lineage linked to criticism of caste barriers and empty ritual. The Pranami tradition developed around Devchandraji's religious centre at Jamnagar and became closely associated with Prannath's teaching and sacred literature.

Both traditions valued devotion and spiritual understanding, but they did not share the same founder, institutional history or central texts.

Prelims focus

  • Kabir emphasised devotion to a formless Supreme Reality and criticised caste pride and external ritualism.
  • The Ravi-Bhan tradition has a historical connection with the Kabir-panth stream in Gujarat.
  • Bhan Saheb was the teacher of Ravi Saheb; the later tradition also includes Dasi Jivan.
  • Devchandraji established Navtanpuri Dham or Khijada Mandir at Jamnagar in 1630.
  • Prannath was Devchandraji's disciple and an important propagator of the Pranami tradition.
  • Trap: The Kabir-related Ravi-Bhan tradition and the Krishna Pranami tradition are not the same sampraday.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, chapter 8, sections A Closer Look: Kabir and New Religious Developments in North India, printed pp. 113–117; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, theme 6, section 8.1, Weaving a Divine Fabric: Kabir, printed pp. 161–162; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Ravibhan Sampraday and Jivan (Dasi); Shri Krishna Pranami Mandir, About Us and Pranami Sampraday History, sections on Devchandraji and Navtanpuri Dham; Shri Krishna Pranami Sampraday, Tartam Sagar, description of the principal scripture; consulted 20 November 2026.]
